authorities.name: Sale of Goods Act 1979, s.14
authorities.date_note: Enactment year. The text verified this session is the current in-force (revised) version. s.14(9) now disapplies this section to consumer contracts (governed instead by CRA 2015 s.9, see consumer-satisfactory-quality.json) - s.14 remains operative for B2B/commercial sales, which is this file's focus.
authorities.proposition: Where a seller sells goods in the course of a business, two terms are implied: the goods are of satisfactory quality, judged by the reasonable-person standard (s.14(2)); and, where the buyer has made known a particular purpose for the goods, that they are reasonably fit for that purpose - unless the buyer does not, or it would be unreasonable to, rely on the seller's skill or judgment (s.14(3)).
authorities.verification_note: Fetched live and directly this session, independently re-fetched and re-confirmed a second time - both fetches consistent on s.14(2)-(3)'s exact text.

authorities.name: Jewson Ltd v Boyhan
authorities.judge_or_panel: Clarke LJ (leading judgment), Sedley LJ, Cresswell J
authorities.proposition: The leading modern authority distinguishing s.14(2) from s.14(3): reliance under s.14(3) can be partial - a buyer may rely on the seller's skill as to the intrinsic qualities of goods while not relying on the seller for a downstream, project-specific characteristic (there, electric boilers' effect on the energy-efficiency ratings of the particular flats they were installed in), meaning no s.14(3) breach where the buyer or their own advisers bore responsibility for that specific question. Under s.14(2), 'satisfactory quality' is assessed against the ordinary/common uses of goods of that type, not against an idiosyncratic purpose peculiar to the buyer's own project.
authorities.verification_note: Fetched live and directly from Find Case Law this session, independently re-fetched and re-confirmed a second time - both fetches consistent on paragraph 60's partial-reliance holding. Cross-checked against swarb.co.uk and a Lexology commentary.

edges.verified_via: Jewson Ltd v Boyhan [2003] EWCA Civ 1030, paras 60 and 69, fetched directly from Find Case Law and independently re-confirmed: construes both s.14(2) and s.14(3), holding neither term was breached on the facts.

what_this_is_not: Two verified nodes covering the satisfactory-quality/fitness-for-purpose distinction in a B2B sale. Does not cover the passing of property/risk, retention of title, agency, or any other Commercial Law subject - all remain unbuilt.
